seo_desc: Rotator cuff tear? Nonsurgical physical therapy in North Palm Beach to rebuild shoulder strength and motion. One-on-one care since 1991. Call 561-624-4263.
lede: Many rotator cuff tears can be managed without surgery, and physical therapy works to rebuild the strength and motion you need to lift, reach and sleep comfortably.
what_it_is: Your rotator cuff is a group of four muscles whose tendons form a cover around the ball at the top of your upper arm bone. Together they keep the ball centered in the shallow shoulder socket and let you lift and rotate your arm. A tear can go partway through a tendon (a partial-thickness tear) or all the way through it (a full-thickness tear). The supraspinatus tendon on top of the shoulder is torn most often.

Some tears happen suddenly, from a fall or a jerking heavy lift. Many more develop slowly as tendons wear with age. Mayo Clinic notes that tears are most common in people older than 50, and painters, carpenters and athletes in overhead sports are more likely to have one. This page covers nonsurgical care. If you have already had a repair, our rotator cuff repair rehab page explains that process.
symptoms: A deep, dull ache in the shoulder
Pain when lifting and lowering your arm
Pain at night that disturbs sleep
Weakness when lifting or rotating the arm
Trouble with overhead tasks such as combing your hair
A snapping feeling and immediate weakness after a sudden injury
causes: Age-related tendon wear, along with reduced blood supply to the tendon
Repetitive overhead work, such as painting or carpentry
Overhead sports such as baseball, tennis and weightlifting
A fall or a sudden, jerking heavy lift
Age over 40, with risk climbing after 50
A family history of rotator cuff problems

how_therapy_helps.intro: Nonsurgical care is the usual starting point. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, about 80 to 85% of patients get pain relief and better function with nonsurgical treatment that includes activity changes and physical therapy. Mayo Clinic describes physical therapy as a typical first-line treatment, with exercises matched to the location of the injury. For partial-thickness tears, the 2025 rotator cuff tendinopathy guideline in JOSPT recommends an active exercise program, which may include motor control and resistance training, as an initial treatment (based on moderate evidence).
methods: Exercises for the rotator cuff and shoulder blade muscles are loaded gradually so your shoulder can lift and rotate with less pain.
Assisted and active motion exercises restore movement lost to pain or guarding and help keep the shoulder from stiffening.
You practice how the shoulder blade and arm move together, so the shoulder makes better use of the strength it has.
Soft tissue work and joint mobilization may reduce pain in the short term, according to the 2025 JOSPT guideline, and are used alongside exercise.
You learn which lifts and overhead positions to limit for now and how to build back up to work, sport and household tasks.

first_visit: Your therapist asks how the pain started, whether there was an injury, and which tasks are hardest. The exam measures active and assisted shoulder motion, compares both arms, and tests rotator cuff strength in different positions. As APTA describes, this includes raising your arm, moving it out to the side and resisting pressure at specific angles. Your plan, and the first exercises, start the same day.
recovery: There is no single timeline for nonsurgical rotator cuff care. Progress depends on the size and type of tear, how long you have had symptoms, and what you need your shoulder to do. Programs usually move from easing pain and restoring motion toward strength, then toward work or sport demands. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons reports that most patients who try nonsurgical treatment improve. Your therapist rechecks strength and motion regularly and keeps your physician informed if progress stalls.
self_care: Stop the activity that caused the pain and avoid movements that clearly hurt.
Limit heavy lifting and overhead reaching for now.
Ice the shoulder for 15 to 20 minutes a few times a day, as Mayo Clinic suggests for minor shoulder pain.
Keep the arm moving gently within a comfortable range so the shoulder does not stiffen.
see_a_doctor: Shoulder pain with trouble breathing, chest tightness or sweating can signal a heart attack. Call 911.
Sudden arm weakness after an injury needs prompt medical attention.
A shoulder that looks deformed after a fall, or that you cannot move away from your body, needs urgent care or an emergency room.
Intense pain or sudden swelling after a fall or accident needs urgent evaluation.
Redness, warmth and swelling around the joint should be checked by a physician.

faqs.q: Can a torn rotator cuff heal without surgery?
faqs.a: Many people regain comfortable use of the shoulder without surgery, even when the tear is still visible on imaging. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons lists rest, activity changes, anti-inflammatory medication, physical therapy and steroid injections as nonsurgical options, and notes that some rotator cuff tears are not painful at all. The goal is a shoulder that works well for your daily life.

faqs.q: Is physical therapy good for a partial rotator cuff tear?
faqs.a: The 2025 rotator cuff tendinopathy guideline in JOSPT, which covers partial-thickness tears, recommends an active exercise program that may include motor control and resistance training as an initial treatment, based on moderate evidence. It also says corticosteroid injections can reduce pain short term but should not be the first-line treatment. Physical therapy is the usual starting point for most partial tears.

faqs.q: What should I avoid with a torn rotator cuff?
faqs.a: Mayo Clinic advises stopping what caused the pain, avoiding painful movements, and limiting heavy lifting and overhead activity for a minor rotator cuff injury. In practice that often means pausing heavy overhead gym lifts and reaching for high shelves while you rebuild strength. Avoiding all arm use is not the goal, because gentle motion helps keep the shoulder from stiffening.

faqs.q: How do I know if my rotator cuff is torn or just inflamed?
faqs.a: The symptoms overlap, so you cannot reliably tell on your own. Both can cause a dull ache, night pain and trouble reaching overhead. Sudden weakness after a fall or heavy lift makes a tear more likely. Mayo Clinic notes that a physical exam plus imaging such as ultrasound or MRI is used to confirm a tear. A therapist's exam can show how much strength and motion you have.

faqs.q: Do cortisone shots help a rotator cuff tear?
faqs.a: They can help some people temporarily. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons reports that a cortisone injection relieves pain in about two thirds of patients for at least 3 months. The 2025 JOSPT guideline says these injections can reduce short-term pain but should not be the first-line treatment. Injections are given by physicians and are often combined with a therapy program.

faqs.q: When is surgery recommended for a rotator cuff tear?
faqs.a: The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says surgery may be recommended when pain does not improve with nonsurgical care, symptoms last 6 to 12 months, the tear is large (more than 3 centimeters) with good surrounding tissue, there is significant weakness and loss of function, or the tear came from a recent injury. An orthopedic surgeon makes that call, often after a trial of physical therapy.

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M75.1 (Rotator cuff tear or rupture, not specified as traumatic) verified on icd10data.com as a category; billing requires a laterality and complete/incomplete subcode. Traumatic tears code under S46.01-.
The JOSPT 2025 guideline covers tendinopathy and partial-thickness tears only; the page does not apply its recommendations to full-thickness tears.
Mayo Clinic says risk rises after 50 while OrthoInfo says after 40; both are attributed or reflected in the causes list.
A higher-quality cohort on full-thickness tears (MOON Shoulder Group, Kuhn et al. 2013) could strengthen the intro, but PubMed/PMC were blocked during research, so it was not cited.

Fact-check 2026-10-07: JOSPT 2025 exercise recommendation is Grade B (moderate evidence), not 'strongest'/'strong evidence'; intro and FAQ corrected. Mayo age wording corrected to 'most common in people older than 50'. Frozen-shoulder attribution to Mayo removed (not found on the cited page).
